newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Emotions abound as New Zealand settles Maori claims.
newsitem.headline: Emotions abound as New Zealand settles Maori claims.

text.p: A quietly emotional ceremony on Saturday marked the settlement between the New Zealand government and a native Maori tribe of land claims dating back 150 years.
"Jim, well...we have done it," a member of the tribe's negotiating team, Charles Crofts, told Prime Minister Jim Bolger after the agreement was signed.
After five years of negotiation, the government on Friday, agreed in principle with the Ngai Tahu (pronounced Ni Taahu) Maori to settle the tribe's claim to large tracts of the South Island.
It denied that the deal, eight days before a general election on October 12, was politically motivated.
Under the settlement, the state will give Ngai Tahu a formal apology and NZ$170 million (US$119 million) in land and cash.

The tribe's grievances date back to 1844 when British colonial authorities bought the first of 10 parcels of land covering most of the South Island for what it now acknowledges was an artificially low price.

Colonial powers went on to acquire 34 million hectares (84 million acres), most of the South Island, for just 14,750 pounds sterling. In one transaction 20 million hectares, or 30 percent of New Zealand's land area, was acquired for 2,000 pounds.
Promises to create reserve lands for Maori were never honoured.

Government representatives and members of the tribe embraced and shed the occasional tear after Treaty Negotiations Minister Doug Graham and Ngai Tahu chief negotiator Sir Tipene O'Regan signed the heads of agreement document on Saturday morning, after a ceremony of speeches, prayers and song.
After the signing, attended by about 100 people, Graham said the process had been one of reconciliation.
"This is the greatest country in the world. We have everything going for us, and it will only be our own stupidity if we do not live in harmony, with respect and dignity.
"I simply want now to wish Ngai Tahu well," Graham said.
O'Regan said the agreement was something the Ngai Tahu could live with and give them a base to build on.
Bolger acknowledged the wrong that had been done to the Ngai Tahu and the significance of this agreement in righting that.
"We have shown that an open chequebook is not needed. What's needed is an open heart," Bolger said.

The government has set aside NZ$1.0 billion to settle all Maori claims. Last year it paid NZ$170 million and returned 15,790 hectares (39,000 acres) of land to the North Island Tainui tribe and earlier this week it settled the Whakatohea claim in the North Island for NZ$40 million.
Hundreds of claims are still outstanding for ancestral land that was seized by colonial settlers.
